ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every image button (`<input type="image">`) exposed to assistive tech has a non-empty accessible name that is also not the browser-supplied default ("Submit Query"). It verifies the name-computation result, not just the presence of an attribute: an `alt=""`, a `name` attribute, or a dangling `aria-labelledby` all leave the element with only the default name and therefore fail. Concretely it walks the input type=image accessible-name algorithm (alt > aria-labelledby > aria-label > title, NOT the `name` attribute) and asserts the result is a meaningful, author-provided string.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 4.1.2's "Name" limb specifically for a user-interface component whose role is button. The image button already has a programmatically-determined role (button) and value semantics; this rule isolates the requirement that its NAME be programmatically determined and non-empty. (The rule is dual-mapped: the same defect is also a 1.1.1 failure because the image button is non-text content, but the 4.1.2 angle is "interactive control must have an accessible name," distinct from the decorative-image alt logic of 1.1.1.)
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any `input` element with `type="image"` that is included in the accessibility tree. Excludes non-image buttons (`
ruleIntents.expectation: Each applicable target must have an accessible name that is neither empty nor the default localized "Submit Query". The supplied failed case has only `name`+`src`; `name` does not contribute to the accessible-name computation, so the name falls back to the default and the expectation fails. Passing requires non-empty alt, aria-label, title, or a resolvable aria-labelledby.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every link exposed to assistive technology has a non-empty accessible name (accName !== ""). It is purely a presence/non-emptiness check on the computed accessible name of link-role elements; it does NOT assess name quality, descriptiveness, or uniqueness. The element must be (a) a semantic link (native a/area with href, or any element with an inheriting link role such as role="link" or role="doc-biblioref"), AND (b) included in the accessibility tree. If both hold, the rule passes iff the computed accName is a non-empty string. The name can come from any source the accName algorithm allows: child text content, alt on a contained img, aria-label, aria-labelledby, or title (on the link or on a child img).
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Name" limb of SC 4.1.2 — specifically the requirement that for UI components, the name is "programmatically determined" (computed and exposed to AT). It does NOT touch the "Role" limb (role is an applicability precondition, assumed correct) or the "Value/States/Properties/notification of changes" limb. It is the most minimal slice: name EXISTS and is non-empty. It deliberately excludes whether the name is correct, meaningful, or matches the visible label (no 2.5.3 label-in-name overlap tested).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any HTML element that is an "inheriting semantic link" AND is included in the accessibility tree. Concretely in the test set: native <a> with an href; <area> with href nested in a map; elements given a link role via role="link" or an inheriting role like role="doc-biblioref". Excluded from applicability: links removed from the a11y tree (display:none, visibility:hidden, aria-hidden=true), elements whose role is overridden away from link (role="button" on an <a>), and elements that never acquire the link role (<a> or <area> with no href).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target element has a computed accessible name that is not the empty string "". Whitespace-only / empty content, decorative-only images (alt="", role="presentation"/"none", empty title), aria-labelledby pointing at empty or non-existent ids, and bare hrefs with no inner text all FAIL because they compute to an empty accName. Note: off-screen/visually-hidden-but-in-tree links (position:absolute;left:-9999px) are still in scope and judged solely on accName, not visibility.

syntheticNarrowness: Every page is a single isolated link on an otherwise empty body — no surrounding navigation, lists, cards, headers/footers, or repeated link groups, so it never exercises a real page where dozens of links coexist and context matters.

All passing names use the exact same well-formed string 'Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI)' or similar; there is no test of borderline names (single space ' ', a non-breaking space, punctuation-only '>>', emoji-only, or whitespace that some engines trim and others don't), even though those are the realistic gray zone for 'non-empty'.

The rule tests only accName PRESENCE, never accName QUALITY — so the corpus has zero 'click here', 'read more', 'link', bare-URL, or 'here' links, which is by far the most common real-world 4.1.2/2.4.4 link defect; a checker could pass every case here while missing the dominant real failure.

Icon-link failures are limited to a stock w3c-logo / act-logo image; no real-world icon fonts (<i class=fa-...>), SVG-as-link (inline <svg> with/without <title>/aria-label), CSS background-image buttons, or sprite-based icons, all of which are the common modern source of nameless links.

Name-source coverage is one example each (one aria-label, one title, one aria-labelledby) and never combines or conflicts them — no test of precedence (aria-label vs visible text), aria-labelledby chaining multiple ids, or aria-label overriding meaningful child text.

No dynamic/interactive scenarios: names are all static at load. Nothing covers links whose accName is populated by JS after render, SPA-router <a>s, links revealed in menus/accordions, or names that change on state (so the harness's vision/tab/focus instrumentation is irrelevant here).

All inapplicable cases use clean single-mechanism removal (one of display:none / visibility:hidden / aria-hidden / role swap); real pages hide links via opacity:0, clip-path, zero-size, off-parent overflow, or conditional CSS, and mix in-tree/out-of-tree state, none of which appear.

Failures are unambiguous empty strings; there are no partially-named or AT-divergent cases (e.g., area-outside-map, presentational-conflict edge cases the rule itself flags as accessibility-support caveats), so the corpus avoids exactly the real ambiguity the rule documents.

Synthetic markup is hand-minified with line-break-split tags and points at local stub image paths that may 404 in the harness — meaning some 'image' links have no real rendered content, which can change whether an engine even computes a name the way a live site would.
Language/i18n is absent: all names are English ASCII; no RTL text, no lang-switched names, no aria-label in another language vs visible text mismatch — common real 4.1.2 considerations.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every WAI-ARIA state/property declared on an HTML or SVG element is one that is PERMITTED on that element, given the element's semantic role (or the ARIA-in-HTML allowances for the host language feature). It is purely an "is this attribute allowed here?" grammar check on the attribute name vs the element/role. An attribute passes if it is (a) a global ARIA state/property, (b) an inherited/supported/required state/property of the element's semantic role, or (c) explicitly allowed on that HTML element per ARIA in HTML. It explicitly does NOT check the attribute's VALUE (e.g. aria-checked="banana" is out of scope), does NOT check whether the name/role/value is actually correct or exposed for the control's purpose, and does NOT require the attribute to be present — only that, if present, it's not prohibited for that role.
ruleIntents.scLimb: Touches the "Value" limb of 4.1.2 only indirectly/structurally: it polices whether ARIA states and properties (the mechanism by which states, properties, and values are programmatically set) are valid for the role, i.e. that author-supplied ARIA can actually be surfaced to AT. The rule's own mapping flags 4.1.2 as a SECONDARY/less-strict requirement: it is primarily a WAI-ARIA 1.2 §8.6 author-conformance rule (and ARIA5 technique), not a direct 4.1.2 outcome. It does not exercise the core Name or Role limbs of 4.1.2 at all, and a 4.1.2 failure does not necessarily follow from a rule failure (a misplaced/ignored ARIA attribute may leave the actual name/role/value perfectly conveyed).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any individual WAI-ARIA state or property attribute (aria-*) that is specified on an HTML or SVG element that is included in the accessibility tree. The unit of test is the single aria-* attribute, not the element. Elements with no aria-* attribute are inapplicable (Inapplicable Example 1: <div role="group"> with no aria attr). Elements removed from the accessibility tree (display:none, etc.) are inapplicable even if they carry a prohibited attribute (Inapplicable Example 2: <div role="button" aria-sort="" style="display:none">).
ruleIntents.expectation: For each in-scope aria-* attribute, at least one of three must hold: (1) GLOBAL — the attribute is a global ARIA state/property allowed on everything regardless of role (aria-busy, aria-label); (2) SEMANTIC ROLE — the attribute is an inherited, supported, or required state/property of the element's computed semantic role (aria-pressed on button, aria-checked required by checkbox, aria-expanded required by combobox, aria-required inherited by switch from checkbox superclass, aria-valuenow/min/max supported by focusable separator); or (3) LANGUAGE FEATURE — the attribute is permitted on that specific HTML element per ARIA in HTML even absent a matching explicit role (aria-required on input type=password). Semantic role is computed AFTER Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution, so role="none" on a focusable button still resolves to button (Passed Example 10). Value correctness is out of scope (aria-expanded="undefined" still passes — Passed Example 8). Fail when the attribute is not allowed for the role/element (aria-sort on button; aria-orientation on audio/application).

Only TWO failing examples and they are both maximally clean single-attribute violations (one prohibited attr on one element); no multi-attribute elements where some aria-* are valid and one is not, which is the common real-world pattern.
Massively imbalanced toward PASS (13 pass : 2 fail : 2 inapplicable) — overfits a checker/LLM toward 'allowed' and barely probes the discrimination boundary.

All examples use a tiny hand-picked vocabulary of roles (button, checkbox, combobox, switch, separator, group, graphics-object) and attributes (aria-pressed, -checked, -expanded, -controls, -label, -busy, -required, -valuenow/min/max, -sort, -orientation); the long tail of ARIA attributes (aria-haspopup, aria-activedescendant, aria-level, aria-posinset, aria-setsize, aria-modal, aria-current, aria-keyshortcuts, aria-roledescription, etc.) and roles (tab, menuitem, treeitem, slider, spinbutton, tooltip, dialog) is untested.

Real misuse is usually accidental and embedded in real widgets (a copy-pasted aria-selected on a button, aria-checked on a link, aria-expanded on a static span); these synthetic cases are author-intent-labeled toy snippets, not the noisy framework-generated markup where these errors actually occur.

Edge cases that make this rule genuinely hard are under-covered: role-changes-with-ARIA-version (combobox aria-controls required in 1.2, not 1.3) is only mentioned in prose; conditionally-permitted attributes appear once (separator+focus) but the inverse (a separator WITHOUT tabindex carrying aria-valuenow, which should fail) is absent; Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution is tested only in the direction that RESCUES an attribute, never the direction where role=presentation legitimately strips it.

No abstract/synonym/superclass roles tested as the literal role (e.g. role=widget, role=input, role=range) nor deprecated/unknown roles; no attribute on an element whose role is computed from a host-language default that has no ARIA mapping besides audio.

Value-out-of-scope is asserted via one contrived aria-expanded='undefined' case; it does not stress that semantically-empty values (aria-sort='') still count as 'specified' in a way a naive checker might skip — only the failing button aria-sort='' shows the empty-string-still-applies behavior, with no passing counterpart.

SC 4.1.2 is the nominal target but the corpus never demonstrates the secondary-requirement caveat the rule itself raises: a failing-rule case that nonetheless satisfies 4.1.2 (the attribute is ignored, the real name/role/value is fine) — so the cases cannot teach the distinction between 'ARIA-conformance failure' and 'actual user-facing 4.1.2 barrier'.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every non-empty, non-whitespace `role` attribute on a visible HTML/SVG element contains at least one token that is a valid, non-abstract WAI-ARIA role (including Graphics and DPUB ARIA role vocabularies). It is purely a token-validity / typo check on the role string: it does NOT check whether the role is allowed on that element type (ARIA-in-HTML), whether the role is appropriate to the widget's actual behavior, or whether name/value are exposed. A single valid token among several passes (fallback-role semantics); all-invalid tokens fail. The classic failure it catches is a misspelled role like `role="lnik"` instead of `link`, which browsers silently ignore so the element falls back to its implicit role.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Role" limb of SC 4.1.2 — specifically that the role of a component is programmatically determinable/correctly exposed via the ARIA `role` attribute. It targets only author-supplied explicit roles via ARIA4 (Using a WAI-ARIA role to expose the role); it does not touch the Name or Value/states limbs, nor implicit/native roles. Note the rule is deliberately STRICTER than the SC: per its own mapping, 4.1.2 is a secondary requirement only, because an invalid explicit role still lets the SC be satisfied by the element's implicit role, so some failed examples may still pass 4.1.2.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any `role` attribute where (a) the value is neither empty ("") nor only ASCII whitespace, AND (b) the attribute is on an HTML or SVG element that is not programmatically hidden. Each qualifying `role` attribute is one test target. Out of scope: missing role attribute, valueless `role`, `role=""`, whitespace-only `role`, and roles on programmatically-hidden (e.g. aria-hidden=true) elements.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each test target (each applicable role attribute) has at least one space-separated token that is a valid value corresponding to a non-abstract role drawn from the WAI-ARIA specifications (core ARIA, Graphics ARIA, DPUB ARIA). One valid token anywhere in the token list satisfies the expectation; an attribute fails only if EVERY token is invalid/abstract.

syntheticNarrowness: Every fixture is a single-element, single-role-attribute snippet; no page has multiple role attributes, nested ARIA structures, or a realistic component (e.g. a tablist/tab/tabpanel set, menu, grid) where role validity interacts with hierarchy.

Invalid roles are only crude lexical typos (lnik) or obvious non-vocabulary phrases (bibliographic-reference). Real-world misuse is broader: abstract roles (role="widget", role="section", role="input"), case/whitespace edge cases (role="Button", role="BUTTON"), dynamically/JS-injected roles, role values templated from data, or roles valid in one ARIA module but not enabled in the document context.

The only programmatically-hidden case is aria-hidden="true"; it never tests CSS display:none, visibility:hidden, the hidden attribute, off-screen positioning, or hidden-via-ancestor — all of which the 'programmatically hidden' definition covers and which exercise the CSS Styling input aspect that fixtures otherwise leave inert.

Fallback-role coverage is minimal: only first-token-invalid+second-valid (searchfield searchbox). It never tests valid-then-invalid ordering, 3+ tokens, duplicate tokens, or an abstract token paired with a concrete one — so the 'at least one valid token' logic is barely stressed.

All roles live on <input> or <span>; SVG elements are in scope per applicability but get zero fixtures, and Graphics ARIA roles (graphics-document, graphics-symbol) are never exercised despite being in the valid vocabulary.

Fixtures are static HTML with no scripting that mutates role at runtime, no Shadow DOM, no iframes, and no author-supplied role colliding with a strong native semantic — none of the conditions that make real-world role validation ambiguous or order-dependent.

The corpus is duplicative rather than diverse (two essentially identical whitespace-only Inapplicable Example 4 fixtures), inflating count without adding a scenario, and the passing examples reuse the exact same searchbox/biblioref content as each other.

Crucially, because the rule is stricter than 4.1.2, none of the 'failed' fixtures demonstrate an actual SC 4.1.2 user-facing failure — they all still have a working implicit role — so the test set never exercises the case where a bad role genuinely removes/changes programmatic role and breaks AT exposure, which is the real WCAG harm.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks one thing only: that every form-field control exposed in the accessibility tree has a non-empty accessible name (after trimming). It is a pure name-presence test for inputs/selects/textareas and ARIA widgets that inherit from input/menuitem/select roles. It computes the ARIA accessible name (label wrapping/for=, aria-label, aria-labelledby, placeholder, text content for elements where content contributes) and fails when that computed name resolves to the empty string "". It does NOT check role correctness, value, name quality/descriptiveness, or whether the name matches a visible label.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Name" limb of 4.1.2 — specifically that a name can be programmatically determined and is non-empty for user-interface components. It does NOT exercise the "Role" limb (a button-like div passes/fails purely on name, role validity is not assessed), nor the "Value/states/properties" limb (e.g. checked/expanded state), nor whether the name is set "in accordance with" the markup language. It only tests existence/non-emptiness of the accessible name, not its accuracy.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to elements included in the accessibility tree that EITHER have one of the form-field semantic roles (checkbox, combobox via select, listbox, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, radio, searchbox, slider, spinbutton, switch, textbox) OR are an input with no semantic role and type color/date/datetime-local/file/month/password/time/week. Excluded: anything not in the a11y tree (display:none, aria-hidden, or role=none/presentation), and control-like roles that do NOT inherit from input/menuitem/select (button, menuitem, option, menu, tree). Disabled fields ARE still applicable (ATs can enumerate them).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope target element has an accessible name that is not the empty string "". A name consisting only of whitespace is trimmed and therefore counts as empty (fails). Native-control labeling mechanisms (wrapping/for= label, placeholder) satisfy it; for ARIA-role-only elements, only ARIA mechanisms (aria-label, aria-labelledby, or contributing text content per the role's name-from-content rules) satisfy it — a native <label> does NOT name a role="textbox" div.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every HTML <summary> element acting as the disclosure control (button) for its parent <details> has a non-empty accessible name. It verifies the control announces a meaningful label — not "" and not just the ::marker triangle pseudo-element — so AT users can identify what the toggle controls. It is purely a Name-presence check on a single native widget type; it does not assess role correctness, value/state exposure, or the quality/appropriateness of the name text.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Name" limb of SC 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) — specifically that a user interface component (the summary disclosure control) has a programmatically determinable, non-empty accessible name. It does not exercise the "Role" limb (the implicit summary/button role is assumed correct, not tested) nor the "Value"/states-and-properties/change-notification limbs (expanded/collapsed state is never checked).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to an HTML summary element only when ALL hold: (1) it is included in the accessibility tree; (2) it functions as the summary button for its parent details element (per browser behavior — effectively the first summary that is a direct child of details, even if not the literal first child node); and (3) it has no explicit role, OR its explicit role is ignored due to a presentational role conflict (e.g. role="none"/"presentation" on a focusable element). Excluded: summary not inside details, not a direct child of details, with an honored explicit role like button (deferred to the Button-name rule), or hidden via display:none (not in a11y tree).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each applicable summary element has an accessible name that is not the empty string ("") and is not merely the name of the ::marker pseudo-element (the disclosure triangle). The name may come from subtree text content, aria-label, or aria-labelledby. Any failing target means SC 4.1.2 is not satisfied; all-pass or inapplicable means the SC needs further testing.

Accessible-name computation is exercised only via the three textbook sources (subtree text, aria-label, aria-labelledby) in isolation; no precedence/conflict cases (aria-label vs text content, aria-labelledby pointing to empty/missing/hidden ids, title attribute as last-resort name, nested labelable content).

Each page contains a single details/summary in a near-empty document; no realistic nesting (details inside nav/article, multiple disclosure widgets, accordion patterns), no surrounding interactive context, no scripts or frameworks that build the summary dynamically.

The ::marker / triangle-only-name nuance called out in the Expectation and Accessibility Support notes is asserted in prose but not isolated by any fixture (no case where the only computed name is the disclosure triangle character across differing user agents).

Role-conflict coverage is a single canonical token (role=none); role=presentation, aria-hidden interactions, or other conflict triggers are absent, and the focusable-but-presentational reasoning is not stress-tested.

Hidden coverage is one mechanism only (display:none on the parent details); other removal-from-a11y-tree paths (visibility:hidden, aria-hidden=true, hidden attribute, off-screen vs truly hidden) are not differentiated.

The 'first summary is the control' rule is shown only with two adjacent summaries; no test for a summary that is interactive-relevant but placed after non-summary content beyond the single Passed Example 4 ordering case, and no malformed/multiple-details edge cases.

Pure native-HTML focus: no custom JS disclosure widgets, no Shadow DOM, no <details> polyfills or ARIA-only (role=button + aria-expanded) accordions — which is where most real 4.1.2 name failures on disclosure controls actually occur, so the corpus underrepresents the SC's real-world failure surface.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that no element carrying aria-hidden="true" contains a focusable inclusive-descendant that is part of the sequential focus (Tab) order. The conflict it catches: AT is told to ignore the element (it's removed from the accessibility tree), yet a keyboard user can still Tab to a focusable control inside it. Such a control is reachable but has no exposed name/role/state to AT, so it is effectively a "ghost" focus stop. The rule resolves this by requiring authors to either (a) keep aria-hidden elements out of the tab order, or (b) not hide tabbable controls. It is deliberately a structural/static reachability check, not a check of whether the name/role/value of the hidden control is correct.
ruleIntents.scLimb: Exercises the implicit "exposed to assistive technology / programmatically determinable" limb of 4.1.2 — specifically that an interactive UI component reachable by the keyboard must have a name, role, and state exposed in the accessibility tree. aria-hidden="true" removes the element from the accessibility tree, so a still-tabbable descendant becomes a focusable component whose role and state are NOT exposed to AT. It is a structural proxy for the "Role can be programmatically determined / States, properties... can be programmatically set and notified" clauses, not the "Name" or "Value change notification" clauses. It does not test name accuracy, value/state synchronization, or custom-widget ARIA correctness.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any element with aria-hidden="true" (literal string value "true", case-sensitive per accessibility-support note). Explicitly inapplicable when the attribute value is anything other than "true": the corpus encodes this via aria-hidden="false" (Inapplicable 2), a valueless/null aria-hidden (Inapplicable 1), and an invalid token aria-hidden="yes" (Inapplicable 3). So applicability is a narrow attribute-presence-and-exact-value gate, not a behavioral one.
ruleIntents.expectation: For each applicable target (aria-hidden="true" element), none of its inclusive descendants in the flat tree may be BOTH focusable AND part of sequential focus navigation. Passing = no such descendant exists. Failing = at least one descendant is focusable and in the tab order. The two conditions are distinct: an element can be focusable but excluded from the tab order (tabindex="-1", Passed 5) and still pass; or it can be removed from focus by being non-rendered (display:none, Passed 2), disabled (disabled, Passed 3), or by a focus sentinel that immediately re-routes focus within 1s (Passed 4) — all of which pass. Note aria-hidden cannot be "un-set" on a descendant: aria-hidden="false" inside an aria-hidden="true" ancestor still fails (Failed 3).
scenarioTypesPresent: Non-focusable hidden content passes (p with aria-hidden=true, no interactive descendant)
Focusable descendant removed from focus via CSS display:none passes
Native disabled attribute removes input from tab order and passes
tabindex=-1 makes a button focusable-but-not-tabbable, passes
Focusable ancestor of an aria-hidden svg is fine (rule only looks downward, not at focusable ancestors)
JS focus sentinel that re-routes focus on focus event passes; the same sentinel with the focus handler removed fails (dynamic/scripted distinction)
Off-screen (position:absolute; top:-999em) link still in tab order fails
aria-disabled (ARIA-only, not native disabled) does NOT remove from tab order, fails

The only interactive element types tested are a, input, button, summary, and a bare tabindex element; real apps hide far richer subtrees (custom comboboxes, menus, carousels, tab panels, video controls, third-party embeds/iframes) behind aria-hidden

The single dynamic case is a hand-coded modal focus-sentinel toggled by one inline script; real-world aria-hidden churn (route changes, modal open/close toggling aria-hidden on siblings, virtualized lists, animation libraries) is excluded — and the rule's own Assumptions section admits it punts on aria-hidden values that change on interaction

Hiding mechanisms are limited to display:none, native disabled, and tabindex; missing: visibility:hidden, hidden attribute, inert attribute, content-visibility, opacity:0, zero-size clipping, and the interaction of CSS-hidden vs aria-hidden together
Only depth-1 or depth-2 nesting is exercised; no deep trees where a focusable element sits many levels below the aria-hidden ancestor, and no multiple focusable descendants under one target
Case-sensitivity is flagged as an accessibility-support concern but is not probed (no aria-hidden='True'/'TRUE' fixture)

The pass/fail distinction in the sentinel pair (Passed 4 vs Failed 6) is invisible in static HTML/markup and DOM alone — it depends on runtime focus behavior — so any static or markup-only checker cannot separate them, yet the corpus presents them as if statically distinguishable

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every iframe element exposed in the accessibility tree has a non-empty accessible name. Concretely: it computes the accessible name of each applicable iframe (via the WAI accname algorithm, where title / aria-label / aria-labelledby are valid sources but the name attribute and src are NOT) and flags the iframe as failing when that computed name is the empty string "" after the accname algorithm's whitespace trimming. It does not check name correctness/descriptiveness, only presence/non-emptiness.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Name" limb of SC 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) — specifically that a programmatically-determinable accessible NAME exists for a user-interface component. It does not touch Role or Value/state-change notification. It targets the embedded-content (iframe) flavor of "UI component" — an iframe is treated as a single focusable/AT-exposed component that an embedding page must label so AT users can identify the embedded document (cf. H64: using the title attribute of frame/iframe).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to iframe elements that ARE included in the accessibility tree, with two carve-outs that make an iframe inapplicable: (a) the iframe has a negative tabindex value, or (b) the iframe is marked as decorative (e.g. role="none"/role="presentation"). Also implicitly inapplicable when there is no iframe at all, or the iframe is removed from the accessibility tree (e.g. display:none, aria-hidden). Deprecated frame/frameset elements are explicitly out of scope. Input aspects required: DOM tree + CSS styling (CSS needed to determine accessibility-tree inclusion).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each target (applicable) iframe element has an accessible name that is not the empty string ("") after accname-algorithm whitespace trimming. Any failing outcome means SC 4.1.2 is not satisfied; all-passed or inapplicable means the SC needs further testing (since this rule only proves name PRESENCE, not adequacy).
scenarioTypesPresent: PASS: accessible name supplied via title attribute (H64 canonical case)
PASS: accessible name supplied via aria-label
PASS: accessible name supplied via aria-labelledby pointing at a visible div's text content
FAIL: name attribute present (name="Grocery List") but name attr is not an accname source, so computed name is empty

FAIL: title="" (explicitly empty title)

syntheticNarrowness: Every test page contains exactly ONE iframe (or zero); never multiple iframes, mixed pass/fail iframes on one page, or nested/cross-origin iframes — real pages embed many third-party iframes (ads, maps, video players, payment widgets, analytics) where only some are named.

The src always points to one tiny local static asset (a 6-item grocery-list document); no real embedded apps, no cross-origin/sandboxed iframes, no about:blank, no srcdoc, no dynamically (JS) injected iframes — yet ad/widget iframes are overwhelmingly script-injected at runtime, which a static-DOM snapshot may miss.

Accessible-name sources are tested only one-at-a-time in isolation (title alone, aria-label alone, aria-labelledby alone); no precedence/conflict cases (e.g. title vs aria-label both present, aria-labelledby pointing at empty/hidden/nonexistent/multiple-ID targets, aria-labelledby + aria-label interaction).

The only failure mechanisms shown are: wrong attribute (name=), missing attribute, empty string, and whitespace-only. Missing are real-world failure flavors like a generic/placeholder name that passes the rule but fails the SC's spirit (e.g. title="iframe", title="frame1", title="advertisement", or an autogenerated GUID title) — the rule deliberately only checks non-emptiness, so these synthetic cases hide that gap.

Emptiness is tested only via ASCII space; no non-breaking space ( ), zero-width characters, RTL/bidi marks, or other Unicode whitespace that may or may not be trimmed by a given accname implementation.

Inapplicability carve-outs are each shown in one clean canonical form (display:none, tabindex=-1, role=none); no compound or ambiguous cases — e.g. aria-hidden="true", visibility:hidden, role="presentation", off-screen positioning, tabindex=-1 combined WITH a name, or an iframe both decorative and focusable — where accessibility-tree inclusion and browser/AT behavior actually diverge (the rule's own Background warns of this inconsistency, but no test exercises it).

All pages are minimal, valid, lang-tagged, single-purpose HTML documents; no surrounding page complexity, no CSS that affects rendering/visibility beyond the one inline display:none / height style, no DOCTYPE/quirks variations, and no realistic layout that could change whether the iframe is actually perceivable.
No deprecated frame/frameset elements appear even as negative/should-be-ignored cases, so the explicit 'frame is out of scope' background note is untested.

scLimbsCoveredByACT: LIMB 1 (NAME can be programmatically determined) — STRONGLY covered. Dedicated non-empty-accessible-name rules for nearly every component type: 97a4e1 (button), c487ae (link, 38 cases incl. role=link, doc-biblioref, image-only-content per F89), e086e5 (form field incl. input/select/textarea/checkbox/date/color), 59796f (image button, input type=image), cae760 (iframe), m6b1q3 (menuitem), 2t702h (summary/details). Name SOURCES exercised: child text content, aria-label (35 uses), aria-labelledby (27 uses, incl. multi-token chains in cc0f0a), title (38 uses), alt (21 uses), <label> wrapping/for. Failing patterns: empty element, name-from-title-only-disallowed, whitespace-only, image with empty alt as sole link content (F89). Directly maps to techniques ARIA14, ARIA16, G108, F68, F89, F111.

LIMB 2 (ROLE can be programmatically determined / is valid) — STRONGLY covered. 674b10 (role attribute has a valid token; failing case uses misspelled role='lnik'), 4e8ab6 (element with role has its REQUIRED states/properties, e.g. role=heading needs aria-level, role=scrollbar needs aria-controls+aria-valuenow), 307n5z (presentational-children role must not contain focusable content), 6cfa84 (aria-hidden subtree must not be in sequential focus order — role/exposure correctness). Implicit/native roles (button, a[href], input) vs explicit ARIA roles (role=button on span, role=link on div) both present. Maps to F59, F42 (emulated links), F15.

STATES & PROPERTIES sub-part of LIMB 3 — PARTIALLY covered, but only the STATIC well-formedness slice. 5c01ea (ARIA state/property is PERMITTED for the role), kb1m8s (ARIA global properties not used where prohibited), 4e8ab6 (REQUIRED states present). State/property attrs that appear: aria-checked(7), aria-expanded(6), aria-controls(6), aria-pressed(3), aria-sort(2), aria-required(2), aria-modal(2), aria-disabled(2), aria-valuenow(3), aria-valuemin/max, aria-orientation, aria-level, aria-live, aria-busy. The corpus checks these attributes are PRESENT, PERMITTED, and VALID-VALUED — not that they reflect actual state or can be set.

Component-type coverage of 'all user interface components' — BROAD. Native (button, a[href], input, select, textarea, summary/details, iframe) AND scripted/custom (role=button/link/menuitem/menu/switch/checkbox/combobox/listbox/option/tab/tablist/dialog/scrollbar/searchbox/textbox/separator on div/span). 'components generated by scripts' partially present via role-on-div/span + onclick link emulation (c487ae Passed Example 2).
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: LIMB 3, 'values that can be set by the user can be programmatically SET' — ENTIRELY ABSENT as a tested limb. No case verifies that a user-settable value/state is actually mutable or settable via the accessibility API. aria-valuenow/aria-checked/aria-selected/aria-expanded appear only as STATIC attributes whose presence/validity is checked (e.g. role=progressbar with fixed aria-valuenow=20 is INAPPLICABLE, role=scrollbar with aria-valuenow=0 just needs the attr present). No slider/spinbutton/editable-combobox where the value is changed and the change is reflected; no <input>/<select>/<textarea> VALUE round-trip is tested (only their NAME). The 'set by the user … can be programmatically set' clause is uncovered.

LIMB 4, 'NOTIFICATION OF CHANGES to these items is available to user agents/AT' — ENTIRELY ABSENT. Trusted Tester Test 2.D (notification of automatic changes via dialog / focus-move / ARIA live region) and technique F79 (focus-change notification) have NO corresponding ACT test case. Only 2 files contain state-mutating script (6cfa84 modal cases), and those mutate style.display / move focus for a focus-trap scenario — they do NOT test change notification. aria-live appears once (kb1m8s) but is tested as a 'global property permitted' case, not as a status/change-notification mechanism. (Note: live-region notification overlaps 4.1.3, handled in a separate lane.)

Failure techniques with NO test-case representation: F15 (custom controls not using an accessibility API at all), F20 (text alternative not UPDATED when non-text content changes — a notification/value-update failure), F79 (focus-state change not programmatically determinable / no notification), F86 (multi-part form field, e.g. split US phone number, where each part lacks its own name) — confirmed zero matches for split/tel/multi-input-sharing-one-label patterns. These F-techniques are listed in the SC inventory but unexercised.

The 'name needs to be VISIBLE' / label-vs-name distinction (Understanding note: 'Occasionally, the name needs to be visible, in which case it is identified as a label') is not isolated — 2.5.3 Label-in-Name interplay (F111: visible label text but no accessible name) exists as a technique but the visible-label-mismatch case is not a dedicated 4.1.2 fixture here.
FRAME (legacy <frame>/<frameset>) — ABSENT. Trusted Tester Test 12.C targets <frame title>, but the ACT corpus only has <iframe> cases (cae760, 4b1c6c); no <frame>/<frameset> fixtures.
contentDomainsPresent: Synthetic single-purpose ACT fixtures only — every page titled 'Passed/Failed/Inapplicable Example N' (79/61/47 split); no real-world page context
Plain text + minimal markup: most cases are 1-3 elements in <body> with no surrounding content
Links: native <a href>, role=link on div with onclick/onkeyup, image-only links, doc-biblioref role
Buttons: native <button>, <input type=image>, role=button on span
Composite/ARIA widgets (mostly as role tokens): menu/menuitem/menuitemcheckbox, combobox/listbox/option, tablist/tab, dialog (modal), switch, checkbox, scrollbar, searchbox, progressbar, separator
Embedded documents: <iframe> with title/aria-label/name (cae760, 4b1c6c duplicate-name pages)

Minimal inline CSS/<style> (7 files) for link-emulation styling and off-screen positioning; one external test-asset uses ::before/::after content
Tiny <script> blocks (2 files) for focus-management in modal/focus-trap cases — not for state-change testing
varietyGaps: BIGGEST GAP: the corpus tests Name + Role (and static state/property well-formedness) but NOT Value-setting or change-notification — i.e. ~half of the SC's normative clause ('values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes … is available to AT') has zero coverage. Every value/state attribute is static; no dynamic/interactive case exercises a value round-trip or a change announcement.

No REAL-WORLD or COMPOSITE pages: all 211 cases are isolated single-component synthetic fixtures. No realistic forms, toolbars, dialogs-in-context, navigation menus with multiple items, or pages combining multiple control types. A model is never tested on finding a name/role defect amid distractor content.

No DYNAMIC / SCRIPTED-state variety: 'components generated by scripts' is named in the SC but only thinly represented (role-on-div + onclick). No JS-built widget whose role/state is set at runtime, no state toggling, no custom control that fails by lacking an accessibility API entirely (F15/F59 under-represented).

Missing component types: <frame>/<frameset> (TT 12.C) entirely absent; multi-part form fields / fieldset-grouped inputs (F86) absent; native interactive elements like <details> beyond summary, <dialog> element (only role=dialog), <progress>/<meter>/<output> native value elements absent.

Name-source edge cases thin: no name-from-CSS-generated-content as the accessible name, no name-from-value (input value as name), limited name-computation-order/precedence conflicts, no recursive aria-labelledby traversal across hidden subtrees, almost no internationalized/non-English names (208/208 lang=en).

Outcome/role imbalance: a few rules dominate (c487ae links 28, 4b1c6c iframes 23, e086e5 forms 22) while value/state rules (5c01ea, kb1m8s) and several SC limbs have few or zero cases; 56 inapplicable cases mostly assert 'no in-scope component present' rather than exercising hard judgment.

aspects.title: Accessible name does not contain the visible label text (F111 / label-in-name overlap, 4.1.2 limb)
aspects.description: A control has BOTH a visible text label AND a non-empty accessible name, but the accessible name omits, contradicts, or wholly replaces the words a sighted user reads on the control. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule (97a4e1 Button, e086e5 Form field, c487ae Link, 59796f Image button, m6b1q3 Menuitem, 2t702h Summary) terminates the instant accName !== ""; none compare the computed name STRING against the rendered visible label STRING. F111 maps explicitly to 4.1.2 (its title is 'Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name') and demands the third check the rules never perform: the accessible name must CONTAIN the visible label, or speech-input users cannot speak what they see to activate the control. Detection requires rendering the page, reading the visible label off the pixels, computing the accessible name, and judging textual overlap — pure visual+semantic comparison, not present in the corpus where any non-empty name is a uniform PASS.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb: the name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rules pass) but fails to be programmatically determinable AS the visible label, so the name does not let an AT/speech user identify and operate the component by its rendered text.
aspects.whyUncovered: The six non-empty-name ACT rules stop at accName !== ""; none of 4.1.2's mapped rules compare the accessible-name string against the rendered visible label string. The corpus contains no fixture where a present visible label and a present-but-divergent accessible name coexist, so a non-empty-but-mismatched name is always a PASS. The string-comparison only lives in 2.5.3 (not in this SC's rule set), and no fully-automated checker reliably extracts the 'visible label' from pixels to compare it, so this needs human visual judgment.

references.quote: Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name
The accessible name contains the text that appears as the visible label.
If check #1 is true, but checks #2 and/or #3 are false, the content fails the Success Criterion.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with a real, populated UI where each control shows visible text but is given an aria-label / aria-labelledby that drops or replaces that text. Render the visible word(s) in normal DOM text so a human (and vision model) reads them off the screen, while the computed accName diverges. Make the divergence the only defect (role and non-emptiness both correct) so every ACT name rule passes. Vary the naming mechanism (aria-label override, aria-labelledby to a hidden node, icon+text child suppressed by a parent name) and the divergence type (omits, contradicts, glyph-only, id-like string).
suggestedScenarios: A toolbar <button>Save</button> overridden with aria-label="Persist document to server" so the visible word 'Save' appears nowhere in the accessible name and a speech user saying 'click Save' fails.
A search field whose rendered <label>Search products</label> is visually present but aria-labelledby points to a hidden node containing only 'query', giving zero overlap with the visible label.
An icon+text link Download PDF with aria-label="document" on the anchor, which suppresses the child text so accName='document' replaces the visible 'Download PDF'.
A 'Next' pagination button visibly reading 'Next' but given aria-label="›" (a chevron glyph) — the accessible name is a character the user can never speak.
A form submit <input type="submit" value="Place order"> with aria-label="checkout-button-3" winning precedence, exposing an internal id-like string instead of the visible 'Place order'.
A cookie-consent <button>Accept all cookies</button> wrapped so aria-labelledby concatenates nodes resolving to 'Cookie banner control', dropping the visible verb phrase 'Accept all cookies'.

aspects.title: Accessible name is present but uninformative / does not communicate the control's purpose (ARIA14 name-quality)
aspects.description: A user-interface control has a non-empty, machine-valid accessible name, but the name does not identify what the control DOES — it is placeholder text, an asset filename, a developer string, or a generic token duplicated across distinct controls. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule is scoped to non-emptiness only and explicitly does not assess descriptiveness, so a name like 'button', 'icon_search_24px.svg', 'TODO label', or five identical 'star' labels passes uniformly. ARIA14 sets the actual bar: 'users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components,' and the Understanding doc requires controls to 'provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies.' Judging adequacy requires inferring the control's function from its icon, position, and behavior, then deciding whether the name conveys that function — semantic judgment no non-emptiness scan performs. (This is distinct from F111: here there may be no visible text label at all; the name is simply meaningless, not mismatched against a visible label.)
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb: the name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rules pass) but does not constitute 'important and appropriate information' identifying the component, so AT users cannot determine its purpose.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT 4.1.2 name rules check non-emptiness only and per the inventory do NOT assess name quality, descriptiveness, or uniqueness; the synthetic fixtures use either one clean correct name or a degenerate empty/default name, never a non-empty-but-useless name (which by rule definition PASSES). Whether a present name actually communicates purpose depends on the control's visual/behavioral identity, which a fully-automated checker cannot reliably infer — it requires human semantic judgment.

references.quote: users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components, in this case “Close”
the controls provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies
Check that the value of the aria-label attribute properly describes the purpose of an element where user input is required

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages of icon-only or custom controls (no visible text label, so F111 does not apply) each given a non-empty name that is semantically empty: generic ('button'), an asset filename, a copy-paste developer placeholder, or one identical token shared across functionally-distinct controls. Make the control's true purpose readable from its rendered icon/position/behavior so a human can judge the name inadequate, while every ACT non-emptiness rule passes. Keep role and states correct so the name is the sole defect.
suggestedScenarios: A toolbar of five icon-only <button>s (cut/copy/paste/undo/redo) each given the identical aria-label="button" — all non-empty, all useless for distinguishing function.
An <input type="image" alt="icon_search_24px.svg"> whose alt is the asset filename: non-empty, passes 59796f, but the name is a path not a purpose.
A 5-star rating widget where each <button> has aria-label="star", so AT announces 'star, star, star, star, star' and the user cannot tell which sets which rating.
An overlay 'Close' <button> whose aria-label was shipped as 'TODO label' — a non-empty developer placeholder that passes automation.
A set of contentEditable <div role="textbox"> fields (address, full name, notes) all sharing aria-label="editor", making them indistinguishable to AT.
A hamburger-menu icon <button aria-label="menu menu"> that opens site navigation — plausible-looking but uninformative duplicated token that does not identify the navigation toggle.

aspects.title: Role is syntactically valid but is the wrong role for the control's appearance/behavior (F15/F59 semantic variant)
aspects.description: An interactive element carries a role that is a real ARIA token (so 674b10 'Role attribute has valid value' passes) and whose required states are present (so 4e8ab6 passes), but the role is WRONG for what the element actually is and does. A sliding toggle switch coded role="checkbox", a control that depresses and fires an in-page action coded role="link", an operable disclosure header marked role="heading", a clickable star coded role="img". F59's literal failure is a div/span with NO role (axe-core flags clickable-with-no-role); the genuinely uncovered, automation-resistant case is a VALID but inappropriate role. Deciding the role is wrong requires seeing the rendered widget, reasoning about its affordance and behavior, and comparing that to the announced role — visual+behavioral judgment, not a token-validity check. The Understanding doc anchors this: when elements 'are programmed... to have a different role and/or function than usual, then additional measures need to be taken.'
aspects.scLimb: The 'Role' limb: the role is programmatically determined and is a valid token (rules pass) but does not correctly convey the component's actual role/function, so AT announces the wrong affordance.
aspects.whyUncovered: 674b10 only checks the role VALUE is a real ARIA token and 4e8ab6 only checks the declared role has its required states present; neither checks the declared role MATCHES the element's visual/behavioral identity. The corpus's role fixtures cover invalid tokens and missing required states, never a valid-but-inappropriate role. A fully-automated checker cannot determine the 'correct' role from rendered appearance and behavior — that is human judgment.

references.quote: interface elements are programmed (in code or script) to have a different role and/or function than usual, then additional measures need to be taken
What roles and states are appropriate to convey to assistive technology will depend on what the control represents.
it is up to the control's author to ensure that the control is correctly exposed to users via the platform's accessibility API

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build custom controls whose visual rendering and JS behavior unambiguously signal one widget type, but assign a different, syntactically-valid ARIA role with that role's required states present (so 674b10 and 4e8ab6 both pass). The rendered affordance must be clear enough that a human/vision model can name the correct role, making the mismatch judgeable. Keep name and state-validity correct so the role choice is the only defect.
suggestedScenarios: A sliding pill toggle switch (thumb + track UI) coded <div role="checkbox" aria-checked="true"> — valid role and required state present, but role mis-describes a switch (should be role="switch").
A pill that visually depresses and fires an in-page action but is given role="link", so AT users expect navigation and instead get an in-page action.
A segmented single-select control where each option is <div role="button"> rather than radio, hiding the mutually-exclusive radiogroup semantics from AT.
An accordion header with a disclosure triangle and expand/collapse behavior marked role="heading" and no button semantics, so an operable control announces as a static heading.
A clickable star-rating widget whose stars are <div role="img"> that respond to clicks — role 'img' is valid but contradicts the interactive rating behavior.
A custom dropdown that visually opens a listbox but whose trigger is role="textbox" — valid role, wrong role for a combobox/button trigger.

aspects.title: Exposed ARIA state/value is present and valid but contradicts the rendered control state (value correctness, not presence)
aspects.description: A custom control exposes a state/value (aria-checked, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-valuenow) that is a permitted, syntactically-valid value (so 4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281 all pass) but that does not match the control's CURRENT visible state: a toggle rendered ON with aria-checked="false", an accordion visibly expanded with aria-expanded="false", a highlighted active tab while aria-selected stays on the first tab, a slider thumb at max with aria-valuenow="0". SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'can be programmatically set' AND that 'notification of changes... is available'; a stale value silently lies to AT. Catching it requires rendering the widget, reading its true visual state, and comparing against the exposed attribute — a visual comparison the static-string ACT rules structurally cannot perform.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Value/State' limb: states and values are programmatically present and valid (rules pass) but do not reflect the component's actual current state, so AT is given an incorrect value and changes are not truthfully reflected.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT state rules (4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281, 5f99a7) check presence, permittedness, and value-validity — all static-string checks. None compare the state value against the actual rendered/interactive state of the widget. The corpus has no fixture where a syntactically perfect aria-checked/aria-expanded/aria-valuenow disagrees with the visual state, because asserting that disagreement requires rendering and visual judgment a fully-automated checker cannot supply.

references.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies
whether or not a checkbox or radio button has been selected, or whether a collapsible tree view or accordion is expanded or collapsed

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render custom widgets in an unambiguous visual state (toggle clearly ON, panel clearly open, tab clearly active, slider thumb clearly at one end) while hard-coding the corresponding ARIA state/value to a valid but contradictory value. Ensure the visual state is the dominant, readable signal so a human/vision model determines the true state, then contrast it with the exposed attribute. Keep role and required-state presence correct so the value-correctness mismatch is the sole defect (no missing-attribute trigger for the ACT rules).
suggestedScenarios: A toggle switch rendered visibly ON (thumb right, green track) but markup hard-codes aria-checked="false" — valid value, wrong state.
An accordion whose panel is visibly open with content showing, but the trigger button retains aria-expanded="false".
A tab strip where the third tab is visually active (underlined/bold) but aria-selected="true" sits on the first tab.
A volume slider whose thumb renders at the far right (max) while aria-valuenow="0" and aria-valuetext is absent.
A mute button visually showing the muted (slashed-speaker) icon but aria-pressed="false", so AT announces 'not pressed' for a muted control.
A multi-select listbox where two options are visually highlighted but only the first carries aria-selected="true".

aspects.title: Accessible name/text alternative on a dynamic named component goes stale after the content changes (F20, temporal correctness)
aspects.description: A named or interactive component whose visual content is swapped by script (a status-icon button, a favorite/star toggle, a refreshable image control, a rotating banner acting as a named region) keeps its accessible name/alt frozen on the OLD content. F20 is explicit: 'the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time.' The name was once correct and is non-empty, so every presence rule passes when sampled once; after the state change it describes a different thing than what is rendered. Catching it requires triggering the change on the page, then comparing the NEW visual to the UNCHANGED name — a temporal + visual judgment no one-shot static scan performs. Scope this to named/interactive components (the 4.1.2 limb) rather than purely decorative images (that angle is 1.1.1).
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name/Value' limb over time: 4.1.2 requires AT 'keep up to date on the status of user interface controls'; a frozen name after a content change means the component's name no longer reflects its current state.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT 4.1.2 fixtures are static single-state snapshots; none mutate component content via script and re-check the name afterward. The non-emptiness rules sample the name once and pass. There is no temporal/diff dimension in the corpus, and F20's failure is fundamentally name-correct-then-stale, which a one-shot automated scan cannot represent — it needs interaction plus before/after visual judgment.

references.quote: the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time. If the text in the text alternative cannot still be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function, then it fails
A Sales chart is updated to October results, but the text alternative still describes September results.
keep up to date on the status of user interface controls in the content

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single self-contained pages that, on a button click or a setInterval/timeout, swap a component's underlying image/src or visual state while leaving its alt/aria-label unchanged. The before and after states must both be screenshot-able (capture focus/click states) so a human can confirm the rendered content changed but the name did not. Favor interactive/named components (toggles, status buttons, refresh controls) to stay in 4.1.2's limb rather than pure decorative images.
suggestedScenarios: A favorite/star toggle whose swaps to a filled star on click but its alt stays 'Add to favorites' (should become 'Remove from favorites').
A weather widget icon button updated from 'sunny.svg' to 'storm.svg' by script, but aria-label remains 'Current weather: Sunny'.
A status indicator that changes from a green 'online' icon to a red 'offline' icon via JS while its accessible name stays frozen at 'User is online'.
A captcha/refresh image swapped on the 'refresh' button click while its alt continues to describe the previous puzzle.
A carousel 'next' control where the active slide src is swapped by setInterval but alt stays 'Slide 1: Spring sale' on slide 3.
A live sales chart whose src is repointed to Q2 data on a button press while alt still reads 'Q1 revenue by region'.

aspects.title: User-settable state/value cannot be programmatically set via AT or its change is not notified (F15, the 'can be set / notification of changes' limb)
aspects.description: SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available' to AT. A custom control can expose a valid role and a valid initial value (so 674b10/4e8ab6/6a7281 pass) yet be uncontrollable or non-reactive for AT: a slider widget that updates aria-valuenow only on mouse drag and never on keyboard/AT activation, a custom switch whose aria-checked never flips when toggled via the accessibility tree, an expander whose aria-expanded never updates when programmatically activated. F15 covers custom controls that 'do so incompletely' — exposing some semantics statically but failing the set/notify contract. Detecting this requires operating the control through the keyboard/AT path and observing whether the exposed value actually changes — interactive behavioral judgment, not a static attribute scan. (Distinct from the stale-value aspect: there the initial value is simply wrong; here the value is initially correct but cannot be changed or its change is never propagated.)
aspects.scLimb: The 'Value can be set + notification of changes' limb: the value is programmatically determinable initially (rules pass) but is not programmatically SETTABLE by the user via AT, and/or changes are not notified to user agents/AT.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT 4.1.2 state/value rules inspect static attribute presence/validity at a single snapshot; none operate the control through the keyboard or accessibility API to verify the value can actually be changed and that the change is reflected/notified. The corpus has no interactive set-and-observe fixture, and a fully-automated checker cannot determine settability/notification without driving the control's interaction and observing AT-visible updates.

references.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build custom controls (switch, slider, expander, tablist) that render and announce a correct initial role + value but wire their state-update logic only to a mouse path (e.g. onmousedown / onclick on a pixel region) with no keydown handler and no programmatic update of the ARIA value. The page should let the tester attempt keyboard/AT operation (focus + Enter/Space/arrow) and observe that the visible UI may move but aria-valuenow/aria-checked/aria-expanded never updates — making the set/notify failure observable. Keep initial role/name/value valid so the gap is purely operability, not presence.
suggestedScenarios: A custom slider that visually moves and updates aria-valuenow only on mouse drag; arrow-key focus does nothing and aria-valuenow stays at its initial value.
A toggle switch whose green/ON visual flips on click but whose aria-checked is hard-wired and never updates when activated via keyboard/AT.
A disclosure widget whose panel opens on click but whose aria-expanded never changes from 'false' regardless of activation method.
A custom select whose aria-activedescendant/aria-selected never updates as options are chosen, so AT is never notified of the new value.
A star rating where clicking sets the visual fill but no aria-valuenow/aria-checked update is emitted, so the chosen rating is never conveyed to AT.
A volume control with +/- buttons that change the displayed number but never update the exposed aria-valuenow or fire any AT-visible change.

aspects.title: Iframe has a non-empty accessible name that does not describe its actual content (TT 12.D)
aspects.description: An <iframe> has a non-empty title / aria-label (so cae760 'Iframe element has non-empty accessible name' passes), but that name does not describe what the frame actually contains — a payment widget iframe titled 'iframe', an embedded map titled 'content', a video-player frame titled 'frame1', or two distinct frames sharing a generic name. Trusted Tester 12.D's pass condition is that 'the combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content' — the tester must look INSIDE the frame and judge whether the name matches. The only iframe rule that goes beyond non-emptiness, 4b1c6c (same-name-must-have-equivalent-purpose), is flagged notFullyAutomatable and covers only the narrow duplicate-name case; nothing covers a single non-empty-but-undescriptive frame name. Judging adequacy requires rendering the frame's content and comparing it to the name — human content judgment.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb for embedded frames: the iframe's name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rule passes) but does not communicate the frame's purpose/content, so an AT user navigating frames cannot identify what each frame is.
aspects.whyUncovered: cae760 checks iframe-name non-emptiness only; 4b1c6c is notFullyAutomatable and only checks that iframes sharing an identical name have equivalent purpose — neither evaluates whether a single frame's name describes its content. TT 12.D requires looking inside the frame to judge descriptiveness, which a fully-automated checker cannot do; the corpus has no fixture pairing a generic iframe name against meaningfully different embedded content.

references.quote: The combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content.
review each frame's corresponding title attribute for a meaningful description of content
the controls provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with one or more <iframe>s in the tab order (no negative tabindex) whose embedded content (use srcdoc for self-containment) is clearly identifiable (a payment form, a map, a video player, a comments thread) but whose title/aria-label is generic or wrong ('iframe', 'content', 'frame', a name describing different content). The tester reads the frame content vs the name to judge the mismatch. Keep names non-empty so cae760 passes and the descriptiveness gap is the sole defect; optionally include a unique-name pair so 4b1c6c does not trigger.
suggestedScenarios: A payment <iframe srcdoc> rendering a credit-card form but titled title="iframe", non-empty yet undescriptive of its content.
An embedded map <iframe srcdoc> showing an interactive location map titled title="content".
A video-player <iframe srcdoc> titled title="frame1" — a number that conveys nothing about the embedded media.
An iframe whose title='Newsletter signup' but whose srcdoc content is actually an advertisement, so the name describes the wrong content.
Two iframes with distinct titles 'Section A' and 'Section B' whose generic names fail to indicate one is a chat widget and the other a help-doc viewer.
A comments-thread <iframe srcdoc> given aria-label='Loading...' (a transient string) that remained after load and no longer describes the comments content.

aspects.title: Each part of a multi-part field has a present but ambiguous/undifferentiated sub-name (F86 semantic variant)
aspects.description: A compound field (US phone as 3 inputs, date as day/month/year, credit card in 4 groups, time as hour/minute/AM-PM) gives EACH sub-input a non-empty accessible name (so e086e5 passes on every part) — but the per-part names fail to convey each part's role within the whole: all three phone parts named 'Phone', a date's three fields all named 'Date', or area-code and prefix both named 'Number'. F86's intent is that without correctly differentiated per-part names users experience 'undefined text fields'; the automation-resistant case is when names exist but are interchangeable/unhelpful. Deciding the sub-names are inadequate requires understanding the compound semantics and the visual grouping (the punctuation/layout that signals 'this is area code, this is prefix') — semantic judgment the per-field non-emptiness rule cannot express.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb at sub-field granularity: each part's name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rule passes) but does not identify the part's specific role within the multi-part whole, so AT users cannot tell which field is which.
aspects.whyUncovered: e086e5 fires only when a sub-field's accName is empty; it cannot judge whether three present names ('Phone','Phone','Phone') collectively fail to identify area/prefix/suffix. F86's requirement is a multi-part SEMANTIC one (each part named for ITS role in the whole) that a per-field non-emptiness check structurally cannot express, and the corpus has no grouped multi-part fixture with present-but-undifferentiated sub-names. A fully-automated checker cannot infer the intended per-part roles from layout.

references.quote: A user with assistive technology will be led to believe that the first field is for the entire phone number, and will experience the second and third fields as undefined text fields.
Check that the value of the aria-label attribute properly describes the purpose of an element where user input is required
some or all of the parts of multi-part form field do not have names

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a populated form with a visually-grouped multi-part field (punctuation/separators making the structure obvious to a sighted user) where every sub-input has a non-empty aria-label/label that is identical or generic across parts, so each part passes e086e5 but collectively the names fail to distinguish the parts. The visual grouping must make the intended per-part roles clear so a human can judge the sub-names inadequate. Keep one fixture as a correct contrast (country-code/area-code/subscriber-number per ARIA14) so the failure is specifically undifferentiated naming.
suggestedScenarios: A US phone field of three inputs visually formatted '( ___ ) ___ - ____' where all three carry aria-label="Phone", giving no area/prefix/suffix distinction.
A date entered as three boxes 'DD / MM / YYYY' where each input is aria-label="Date", so AT cannot tell day from month from year.
A credit-card field in four 4-digit groups where every group is aria-label="Card number", indistinguishable to AT.
A time field hour/minute/AM-PM where the hour and minute inputs are both aria-label="Time" and the AM-PM select is unlabeled-but-titled 'Time'.
A phone field where the area-code input is aria-label="Number" and the prefix input is also aria-label="Number", duplicating a generic token across parts.
A SSN-style three-part field 'XXX-XX-XXXX' where each segment shares aria-label="SSN" with no first/middle/last group differentiation.

pages.scenario: SaaS document-editor toolbar: the primary action button visibly reads 'Save' but carries aria-label='Persist document to server', so the visible word 'Save' appears nowhere in the accessible name. Verified in Chromium: role=button, accName='Persist document to server'.
pages.mechanism: aria-label on a native <button> overrides and suppresses the child text node 'Save'; the accessible name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role is correct, but it omits the visible label, so a speech-input user saying 'click Save' matches nothing and a screen-reader user gets no anchor to the on-screen word. F111 check #3 (accName must contain the visible label) fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT rule 97a4e1 terminate at accName !== ''; none of 4.1.2's mapped rules extract the rendered visible label 'Save' from pixels/DOM and compare it to the computed name string (that string-overlap check lives only in 2.5.3). aria-label is well-formed, so no empty/missing-attribute lint fires; catching it needs a human to read 'Save' and judge it absent from the name.

citation.quote: For all controls with a visible label (e.g., link text, button text, programmatically linked label, images in links or buttons with text, etc.), check that: 1. The control has a visible text label. 2. The control has an accessible name. 3. The accessible name contains the text that appears as the visible label.

pages.scenario: Pharmacy search field with a real visible <label for='med-search'>Search medications</label>, but the input also has aria-labelledby pointing to a visually-hidden node containing only the back-end query key 'rx-query'. The explicit aria-labelledby wins over the <label>. Verified in Chromium: role=searchbox, accName='rx-query' (zero word overlap with the visible label).
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby is consulted before the <label> association in the accessible-name computation, so the visible 'Search medications' is discarded and the name becomes the internal slug 'rx-query'. Name is non-empty (e086e5 passes) and role correct, but it shares no words with the visible label, so voice users cannot speak it and screen-reader users hear a meaningless field name. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse confirm a non-empty name and stop. The aria-labelledby IDREF resolves to a real present element, so the dangling-reference lint does not fire. No checker reads the visible <label> text off the rendered page and diffs it against 'rx-query'; recognizing the name is a telemetry key rather than the on-screen label is a semantic judgment.

citation.quote: If check #1 is true, but checks #2 and/or #3 are false, the content fails the Success Criterion.

pages.scenario: Government fiscal-office page listing property-tax PDFs. The first download link is an <a> containing a PDF icon plus visible text 'Download PDF', but a reusable-component placeholder aria-label='document' was left on the anchor, suppressing the child text. Verified in Chromium: role=link, accName='document' (the other rows, with no aria-label, correctly name themselves by their visible text).
pages.mechanism: aria-label on the anchor wins over its descendant text, so the icon+text child 'Download PDF' is not contributed to the name; the generic 'document' wholly replaces the visible label. Name is non-empty (c487ae passes) and role correct, but in a links list the user cannot distinguish or voice-target it. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: c487ae and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a non-empty link name and pass; 'document' is a plausible real word with no empty/dangling attribute to lint. Detecting the failure requires reading the visible 'Download PDF' off the rendered row and recognizing the programmatic name 'document' neither contains nor describes it — a visual+semantic comparison no automated 4.1.2 checker performs.

citation.quote: When speech input users interact with a web page, they usually speak a command followed by the reference to some visible label (like the text in a button or a link, or the text labelling some input). If the control lacks an accessible name, speech users won't be able to activate the control using its visible label.

pages.scenario: Literary-magazine pagination (page 2 of 9). The forward control visibly reads 'Next' plus a decorative chevron, but aria-label='›' (U+203A, single right-pointing angle quotation mark) was set on the anchor, replacing the visible word with a lone unspeakable glyph. Verified in Chromium: role=link, accName='›'.
pages.mechanism: aria-label overrides the child text 'Next', leaving the accessible name as a single punctuation glyph. It is technically non-empty (c487ae passes) and role correct, but a screen reader announces a symbol name or nothing, and a speech-input user has no spoken token for '›', so the control is unreachable by voice and the visible label 'Next' is absent from the name. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The name is a non-empty string, so c487ae / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse pass; none classify whether the name is a single non-speakable glyph that fails to match the visible word 'Next'. That requires reading the rendered 'Next' and a human visual+linguistic judgment that '›' is neither the visible label nor a speakable name.

citation.quote: Success Criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value requires a programmatically determinable name for all user interface components. Names may be visible or invisible. Occasionally, the name needs to be visible, in which case it is identified as a label.

pages.scenario: Renters-insurance quote wizard (step 3 of 3). The final action is a native <input type='submit' value='Get my quote'> so the button face reads 'Get my quote', but a form-builder integration emitted aria-label='quote-submit-btn-v2' (the component's internal id), which overrides the value. Verified in Chromium: role=button, accName='quote-submit-btn-v2'.
pages.mechanism: For a submit input the value normally becomes the accessible name, but aria-label takes precedence and replaces it with a hyphenated developer slug. Name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role correct, but a screen reader reads an internal identifier and a speech-input user saying 'click Get my quote' cannot activate it. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 97a4e1 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse confirm a non-empty name and pass; 'quote-submit-btn-v2' is a valid string with no empty or dangling attribute to lint. Recognizing the programmatic name is an internal id rather than the rendered 'Get my quote' requires reading the button face and judging the string mismatch — overlap logic that lives only in 2.5.3, not in this SC's rule set.

citation.quote: When standard controls from accessible technologies are used, this process is straightforward. If the user interface elements are used according to specification the conditions of this provision will be met.

pages.scenario: French bistro reservation panel (<html lang='fr'>). The primary button visibly reads 'Réserver une table', but aria-labelledby concatenates two visually-hidden untranslated English nodes ('Confirm' + 'booking'). Verified in Chromium: failing button role=button, accName='Confirm booking'; a co-located passing twin 'Annuler' computes accName='Annuler la réservation' (contains the visible word), included as a boundary contrast.
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby overrides the button's own French text and concatenates the referenced hidden nodes, so the accessible name is English 'Confirm booking' on a French page — a language switch with zero word overlap with the visible 'Réserver une table'. Name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role correct, but a French voice-control user saying « Réserver une table » activates nothing and a screen reader contradicts the visible label. The passing twin's name is a superset of its visible 'Annuler', satisfying F111 check #3; the primary control fails it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both buttons have non-empty names, valid aria-labelledby IDREFs resolving to present elements, and valid roles, so 97a4e1 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse pass both. No automated 4.1.2 checker reads the visible French label off the rendered button, detects the language switch to English, and diffs it against 'Confirm booking'. Judging the name is in the wrong language and omits the visible label is a human visual+linguistic decision.

pages.mechanism: Three split-phone <input>s each have a non-empty accessible name 'Phone' (so e086e5 passes per-field), but the three identical names do not identify which box is the area code, the prefix, or the four-digit line number; the disambiguating '( ) -' punctuation is in aria-hidden spans. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse implement ACT e086e5, which fails a field only when its accessible name is EMPTY. Detecting the defect requires recognizing the three inputs are one compound phone field, reading the visual '( ) -' grouping to infer per-part roles, and judging that three interchangeable 'Phone' names fail to differentiate them — multi-part semantic + visual reasoning a per-field non-emptiness check structurally cannot express.
