finalReport.title: Name, Role, Value

problems: PROMPT/FILE METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): the task prompt describes a 'Save' button with aria-label='Persist document to server', cites F111, and gives selector 'button.tbtn.primary' under slug 'name-omits-visible-label-text'. The ACTUAL on-disk case-01.html/.md is a completely different scenario: a 'PaleoCon 2026' workshop booking grid whose checkbox input[name=bk-paleo] is named (via aria-labelledby) for the WRONG cell, cited to ARIA9. I evaluated the real files. The harness/orchestrator metadata for this case is stale and should be reconciled before use.

Selector in prompt (button.tbtn.primary) does not exist on the page; the real element under test is input[name="bk-paleo"]. Geometry confirms it renders in the 'The Paleozoic era' cell (x=173,y=256) while its accName is 'Track 2 2 to 5 PM The Cretaceous period Attend'.

Minor SC-theory nuance (does not change the verdict): ARIA9 is a *sufficient* technique, so failing its procedure does not by itself prove the SC fails. The case is nonetheless a genuine 4.1.2 Name-limb failure (name is determinable but semantically wrong for this control, and it collides identically with the real bk-cretaceous checkbox so the Paleozoic session has no uniquely-named control). The .md itself flags the judgment call and correctly distinguishes it from 2.5.3.

PROMPT/MANIFEST MISMATCH (the dominant problem): the orchestration prompt describes a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT page than what is on disk. Prompt claims a government fiscal-office page with property-tax PDF download links, an <a> with PDF icon + visible 'Download PDF' text, aria-label='document' suppressing child text, selector 'a.docrow[aria-label]', mechanism = aria-label overrides descendant text, citation = F111. The actual case-03.html is a Meridian Utilities billing table with three <button> Pay controls, mechanism = aria-labelledby off-by-one referent, citation = ARIA16. grep for 'docrow', 'aria-label=', 'Download PDF', and '<a ' in the HTML all return ZERO matches (exit 1). The prompt's selector a.docrow[aria-label] matches NOTHING in this file.

The prompt's claimed citation (F111) is the WRONG technique for the actual defect: F111 covers a control that LACKS an accessible name ('If the control lacks an accessible name, speech users won't be able to activate the control'). Here the button HAS a non-empty name; the name is wrong/misidentifying, not absent. The F111 quote does appear verbatim in wcag-techniques/failures/F111.html, but it does not support this page's actual mechanism.

Minor doc-internal nuance: the .md frames the outcome as 'failed' under F111 #3 being 'technically true' yet 4.1.2 violated; the cleaner basis is ARIA16 check #2 (which the .md itself also cites verbatim and correctly). The 4.1.2 failure is real either way.

Minor scope nuance (not a defect): F111 is a failure of SC 1.3.1, 2.5.3 AND 4.1.2 jointly; the 'visible label absent from accessible name' mechanism maps most directly to 2.5.3 (Label in Name), which is partially automatable. The md's framing that this is purely 4.1.2 and that automated tools 'miss it' is true only for 4.1.2's own coverage (link-name/button-name pass a non-empty name); a 2.5.3 Label-in-Name checker could partially detect the visible-text-absent aspect. Filing under 4.1.2 is still defensible and supported by the citation + F111.
Citation grep failed on a single-line search only because the quoted sentence wraps across reference lines 47-50; the text is present verbatim modulo whitespace/line-wrap. Not a real defect.

Incidental, SC-unrelated axe violations present on the page (color-contrast on .legal small text, missing main landmark, region/landmark) — noise unrelated to the 4.1.2 element under test, but worth knowing they exist when this page is scored.

The anti-pattern is canonically a 2.5.3 (Label in Name) failure; the doc honestly acknowledges this and maps to 4.1.2 via F111. The mapping IS valid (F111 is officially a failure of 1.3.1/2.5.3/4.1.2), but a strict reader of 4.1.2's normative text alone (name present + role correct = literal pass) could argue the 'pure' 4.1.2 angle is weaker than 2.5.3 — keep this in mind if the corpus wants single-SC purity.

Minor doc/citation mismatch (not a defect): the .md headlines ARIA16 as the Citation but the actual distinguishing logic (visible-label vs accessible-name containment / 'check #3') comes from F111, not ARIA16. ARIA16 check #2 ('the referenced element accurately labels the control') is genuinely relevant and the quote is verbatim, so the citation is sound — but F111 is the more precise authority for the failing comparison and the doc relies on it in the mechanism while citing ARIA16 in the Citation header. No factual error, just split attribution.

Pedantic SC-scoping note: 'name omits visible label text' is most squarely 2.5.3 Label in Name (F111 covers 1.3.1/2.5.3/4.1.2 jointly). The corpus files it under 4.1.2, which is defensible because the accessible name programmatically contradicts the perceivable control identity, and F111 explicitly lists 4.1.2. Not a defect, but the case sits on the 2.5.3/4.1.2 boundary.

Minor: 'button' as an accessible name is arguably semi-detectable as an anti-pattern (accessible-name equals the implicit role token), so a future heuristic could partially flag it; however no shipping checker (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) flags name==role for native <button>, and distinguishing five distinct functions sharing one generic name is fundamentally a semantic judgment — requiresHumanJudgment still holds.

SC-boundary borderline (not a defect, but worth noting): under a strict literal reading, 4.1.2 only requires a name that is programmatically determinable and non-empty — which all three buttons satisfy. The 'name does not convey purpose' aspect lives at the edge of 4.1.2 and overlaps 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels). The corpus folder name ('name-present-but-not-descriptive-of-purpose') and WCAG Understanding 4.1.2 do support treating a meaningless leaked key as a 4.1.2 failure, so the label stands, but the case sits on the SC interpretive boundary by design.

Citation tangentiality (minor): ARIA14's quoted sentence is verbatim and correct, but ARIA14 describes the legitimate technique of naming via aria-label — which the page actually used. The failure is about name QUALITY, not the naming mechanism, so the technique is supporting/contextual rather than directly diagnostic of the failure. Not a hallucination.

Subjective edge (not a defect, a caveat): a checkbox visually styled as a toggle is sometimes treated as an acceptable pattern since `checkbox` is the superclass of `switch`; a lenient reviewer could call this borderline rather than a clear fail. The page mitigates this with unambiguous switch styling (sliding pill, grey->green) plus explicit instant-effect framing ('Changes apply instantly', 'Saved automatically'), so the role-mismatch judgment is well-supported. Recorded for transparency only.

Minor (not a defect): the selector .cta[role="link"] matches BOTH the Starter ghost pill and the Pro pill; the inspect tool's single-element 'query' block resolved to the Starter element first. The doc nominally names the Pro CTA as element-under-test, but both pills carry the identical defect, so the page is internally consistent.

Minor design note: the keydown handler binds Enter only (no Space), explicitly to mirror link semantics. This is intentional per the source comment and actually reinforces the mis-coding, but it means the control is not fully button-operable either — a secondary consequence not called out as a separate finding in the doc.

Minor (non-defeating): the .seg wrapper has aria-labelledby="unit-lbl" which makes the AX node a NAMED generic ('Temperature unit', backendNodeId 17) rather than an unnamed one. It is still not a group/radiogroup role, so it does not rescue the missing single-select group semantics — but the doc/comment describe the wrapper as 'plain ... no group role', which slightly understates that AT does at least announce a (non-grouping) named container around the two buttons.

Minor name-cleanliness imperfection (does not undermine the case): the disclosure-triangle glyph is not aria-hidden, so the accessible name includes it -- AX tree shows name '▸ Do you offer weekend appointments?' instead of the clean question text. The case is about the role mismatch, not the name, so this is cosmetic but worth noting.

Documentation slightly over-claims that aria-expanded is merely 'poorly surfaced'; the Chromium AX tree shows it is in fact NOT exposed at all on the heading node (no expanded/collapsed property), which actually strengthens the failure but means the doc's wording understates it.

Minor citation-fit caveat: the prompt's named citation F15 ('custom controls that do not use an accessibility API ... or do so incompletely') is exemplified in F15.html by a control that exposes NO accessibility info at all (the music-player example). Here a role IS exposed via ARIA -- it is simply the WRONG role (img on an operable control). This is a 'do so incompletely/incorrectly' reading of F15 rather than its literal 'no exposure' example; a wrong-role-specific reference would be a tighter fit. Mitigated because the .md pairs it with the WCAG NRV Intent quote (verbatim at name-role-value.html line 21), which directly covers 'AT can gather appropriate information about, activate (or set) ... user interface controls.' Both quoted sentences verify VERBATIM (F15.html line 12; name-role-value.html line 21).

Minor (out-of-scope for 4.1.2): the doc claims de-DE locale but the page declares <html lang="en"> (line 2). The inspect tool confirms lang="en" while all content/accessible names are German. This is an SC 3.1.1 lang-of-page mismatch, not a 4.1.2 Role-limb concern, and does not affect the passed outcome under the SC being tested.

Cosmetic: the disclosure button's accessible name is computed as 'Mehr Optionen ▾' (it absorbs the chevron glyph ▾ into the name) rather than the cleaner 'Mehr Optionen' the doc implies; harmless for 4.1.2 since role/state are still correct, but the chevron should ideally be aria-hidden.

Minor realism leak (does not affect SC verdict): the page bakes its own test rationale into rendered content/comments — the .note div (HTML lines 77-82, present in the AX tree as visible StaticText), the inline comment on line 48 ('Rendered ON ... But aria-checked is hard-coded false'), and the script comments lines 90-91 all narrate the intended defect, which breaks the realistic-page illusion an adversarial reviewer expects.

Borderline automated-detectability nuance: the visual ON state is driven by a statically-named CSS class '.is-on' present in source markup; a bespoke heuristic that correlates a semantically-loaded class name with aria-checked could in principle flag it without rendering. No shipping checker (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse/ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281) does this, so the case still legitimately needs human/vision judgment, but the static class name makes the 'undetectable' framing slightly weaker than a render-only contradiction.

Secondary citation F20 is an imperfect analogy: F20 is titled 'Failure ... due to not updating text alternatives when changes to non-text content occur' and is scoped to text alternatives for non-text content (image alt/value), NOT to aria-expanded state values. The exposed-state contradiction here is governed by Name/Role/VALUE (state correctness), not by F20's stale-text-alternative shape. The .md acknowledges the stretch ('F20 is the canonical "exposed value left stale" failure shape'), but it is not a precise technique mapping. The primary citation (Understanding 4.1.2) is exact and fully on-point, so this does not invalidate the case.

The F20 quote 'the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time.' matches F20.html (lines 7-8) only as a fragment lifted from mid-sentence ('...occurs when non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time'); the leading 'the' is added. Whitespace/fragment-level discrepancy, not a fabrication.

Secondary citation (Understanding 4.1.2 'Intent' quote in the .md) could not be source-verified in refs/ — no name-role-value.html Understanding doc is present in the repo. This is the .md's secondary citation only; the PRIMARY task citation (refs/trusted-tester/sc-4.1.2-name-role-value.md) is verified verbatim and supports the mechanism, so the case is not blocked. Minor documentation gap only.

Citation precision (minor, non-blocking): the 'Claimed citation' G108 quote 'allow user-settable properties to be directly set, and provide notification of changes' is verbatim and correctly attributed (line 1 / h1 of wcag-techniques/general/G108.html), but it is pulled from the technique TITLE and G108 is a *sufficient* technique about ENABLING settability/notification — slightly tangential to this defect, which is a value-CORRECTNESS lie on initial paint. The mechanism is actually carried by the doc's primary SC-4.1.2-text citation (verified verbatim in refs/trusted-tester/sc-4.1.2-name-role-value.md lines 4-7), so this does not change the outcome.

Tab-order note (not a defect): inspect.js shows the slider focusable at stops 3/8/12/17/21 with body/none wraps in between — this is the harness's tab loop, not a focus-order problem; slider is correctly reachable via tabindex=0.

Minor corroboration caveat (not a defect): Chromium's Accessibility.getFullAXTree does NOT serialize aria-sort into the columnheader properties array (props are only readonly/required for all four headers). aria-sort is exposed at the platform-AT layer (AX API / IAccessible2 object attribute) and JAWS/NVDA announce it, but the CDP full-AX-tree is not a faithful oracle for this property. AX-tree corroboration is therefore partial: it confirms role=columnheader and name='On-time %' but cannot confirm the wrong sort value. The DOM/IDL is unambiguous: aria-sort attr='ascending', th.ariaSort='ascending', arrow='▼' (down, aria-hidden=true so AT gets no arrow), first row 96.8% / last row 71.2% (descending). The realness of the AT-perceived failure relies on the screen reader announcing aria-sort, which JAWS/NVDA do — a reasonable assumption.

The task prompt's 'Claimed citation' field lists only the Understanding quote; the .md additionally cites the trusted-tester SC text. Both verify (see cdpEvidence). Not a problem — flagged only for completeness.

Minor (not a case defect): the selected-state check mark is generated via ::before { content:"\2713" } and Chromium folds it into the accessible name (AX names are '✓ Go' / '✓ PostgreSQL' rather than 'Go' / 'PostgreSQL'). Cosmetic name pollution; does not affect role=option or the selected value, so 4.1.2 still passes, but the .md's claimed announcement 'Go, selected' is slightly idealized vs. actual '✓ Go, selected'.

Out-of-scope observation: the listbox sets aria-activedescendant and has a .focused style, but the only JS handler is 'click'; there is no keydown/arrow-key handler, so keyboard navigation among options is not actually wired. Irrelevant to the 4.1.2 pass discriminator (state truthfulness), but the component is not fully APG-operable as the persona text implies.

Minor scope overlap (not a defect): the post-click favorited state also has aria-hidden="true" on the #savedNote, which arguably implicates SC 4.1.3 (Status Messages) for SR users; however the SC-under-test failure (stale accessible name on the interactive toggle) is the clean, correct 4.1.2 limb, so the label is right and the overlap does not warrant a change.

axe-core is not installed in the repo, so the static-scan corroboration was reasoned rather than executed; the CDP AX tree (valid named button in both states) and code review fully support the 'static scanners pass' claim, so this is not a verdict risk.

Minor classification nuance (not a defect): F20's canonical/primary SC is 1.1.1 (the F20 title reads 'Failure of Success Criterion 1.1.1 and 4.1.2'), and the page's own HTML comment leads with 'SC 4.1.2 (with 1.1.1)'. A purist could argue this sits more naturally under 1.1.1. The 4.1.2 anchoring is still defensible: the img alt IS the element's accessible NAME, and that name going stale relative to the component's current rendered value is a legitimate Name/Role/Value concern. The 'failed' outcome is correct under either co-cited SC.

PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): the prompt's claimed scenario describes an Arabic RTL developer-forum flag/report toggle with selector 'button#flagBtn > svg > title#flagTitle' and Arabic strings, but the actual case-05.html is an English (lang=en) Tideline music-player ICON-ONLY repeat-MODE 3-state cycle button with selector 'button#repeatBtn > svg > title#repeatTitle'. The prompt selector does not exist in the file. I evaluated the actual page, which is internally consistent with its own .md and citation.

Minor: reviewers relying on the orchestrator's prompt metadata would be testing a non-existent element; the corpus row's prompt-level scenario/selector should be regenerated to match the real repeatBtn case.
None material. This is a deliberate BOUNDARY/PASSED case, so 'errorIsReal=false' is the INTENDED state (no accessibility defect exists), not a defect in the case itself.

Minor: the .md citation header labels the source slightly loosely ('WCAG Technique F20, Tests - Expected Results') but the quoted sentence itself is verbatim and correctly attributed to wcag-techniques/failures/F20.html (Expected Results list item).

Cosmetic only (not a page defect): inspect.js/CDP console output renders the em-dash in aria-valuetext as mojibake ("30 â Conservative"); the actual DOM value is the correct UTF-8 em-dash ("30 — Conservative"), verified by direct getAttribute in the Puppeteer probe. This is a tooling console-encoding artifact, not an issue with the page.

Minor: the F15 citation in both the task prompt and the .md doc begins the quote at "When custom controls are created..." but the source (wcag-techniques/failures/F15.html line 11) actually reads "However, when custom controls are created...". The quoted text is verbatim from "when" onward and is not misattributed or stitched; dropping the leading "However," and capitalizing "When" is a benign truncation, not a defect that changes meaning.
Note (not a defect): the second .md citation (wcag-understanding/name-role-value.html, lines 41-43) also verifies verbatim and correctly supports the 'control states must be exposed/updated' point.

Signal caveat: Chromium CDP getFullAXTree does not surface the aria-sort `sort` property on these columnheaders (only readonly/required in properties[]), so the CDP tree cannot directly corroborate the frozen-state claim; verification rests on the DOM aria-sort attribute (confirmed frozen by my Puppeteer operate-then-observe probe) plus how real AT reads the platform a11y API. Not a defect in the case, but the inspect.js AX dump is non-corroborating on this exact attribute.

Minor (non-blocking) cosmetic note: the raw tab order shows TWO iframe tab stops (stops 4 and 5, repeating at 11/12, etc.), which on first read could appear to contradict the doc's 'single iframe' claim that makes ACT rule 4b1c6c inapplicable. Verified this is NOT a second iframe element: the DOM has exactly one <iframe> (document.querySelectorAll('iframe').length === 1); the second tab stop is Chromium descending into the single iframe's about:srcdoc document, whose role=application map contains two focusable aria-labelled Zoom +/- buttons. The 'single iframe / 4b1c6c inapplicable' claim is therefore correct. No fix required; noting only so a reviewer isn't misled by the tab dump.

Tab-order signal from inspect.js is noisy/misleading on its face (24+ 'iframe' stops with role:null), but the page source contains exactly ONE <iframe> element (AX tree backendNodeId 21); the repeated stops are the tool cycling the single frame's internal focus + the file:// address bar. Does not affect the verdict, noted only so a reader does not misread it as multiple iframes.

Minor SC-scoping nuance: 'accessible name describes the wrong content' is, strictly, exposed via WCAG 4.1.2 only because Trusted Tester folds iframe-name-quality into Test 12.D; a pure ACT cae760 check passes. The page and doc handle this correctly and the citation is accurate, so this is a framing note, not a defect.

Minor citation-form note (not a defect): the quoted 4b1c6c Applicability sentence is not a literally contiguous string in act-rules/extracted/4b1c6c.md — the extracted markdown inserts list-bullet markers ('- ') before each clause ('- are in the same web page (HTML) ; and - are included in an accessibility tree ; and - that have matching accessible names...'). After whitespace/bullet normalization it matches verbatim (wording, punctuation, and the '( "" )' notation are identical), so it is within the allowed whitespace tolerance and correctly attributed. Worth recording only because the quote is presented as 'verbatim'.

F86's LITERAL test procedure (refs lines 35-42: 'Check that there is a programmatically determined name for the field; failure applies only if check #1 is FALSE for any subfield') actually PASSES this page, because all three inputs DO have a programmatically determined name ('Phone'). F86 as written targets ABSENT sub-field names; this page has PRESENT-but-identical names. The doc is candid about this (md lines 17/41, html comment lines 12-17) and labels it an 'F86 semantic variant — present-but-undifferentiated'. The 'failed' outcome is therefore an intent-based EXTENSION of F86, not its literal procedure. A strict purist could argue the inadequate-name defect maps better to 3.3.2 (Labels or Instructions) / 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) than to 4.1.2, since name+role+value are all programmatically determinable. The mapping to 4.1.2-failed is defensible (the F86 prose on html line 14 describes exactly this experiential failure, and ARIA14's phone example is the canonical fix in the 4.1.2 space), but reviewers should note the literal-procedure mismatch.

Minor: the cited F86 quote ('three undefined text fields') describes the case where fields have NO name at all; on this page the AT user hears 'Phone, Phone, Phone' (named but not differentiated), not '(' / ')' / '-'. The verbatim quote is real and supports the SPIRIT of the failure, but the literal phenomenon it describes (punctuation read as field names) does not occur here because the punctuation spans are aria-hidden and absent from the AX tree.

Citation fit (minor): the verbatim primary quote describes a STRONGER defect (no name at all -> 'three undefined text fields') than the page exhibits (three valid-but-identical 'Date of birth' names). The page's fields are NOT undefined, so F86's literal test procedure ('fail if any subfield has no programmatically determined name') would technically PASS this page. The doc is honest about this ('F86 semantic variant', e086e5 passes per-field), but the quote slightly over-claims by mapping an absent-name example onto an identical-name case.

F86 never covers identical/non-distinguishing names (grep: no 'identical'/'same name'/'distinguish'/'generic' in F86.html); the 'failed' verdict rests on 4.1.2 INTENT rather than the cited technique's literal scope. Defensible but adversarially debatable — could be reframed/strengthened with a citation that actually addresses shared/ambiguous names rather than missing ones.

Citation is a SEMANTIC EXTENSION of F86, not a literal application. F86's procedure (verified verbatim at wcag-techniques/failures/F86.html lines 35-37) is binary: 'For each subfield in the multi-part form field: Check that there is a programmatically determined name for the field' and 'If check #1 is false for any subfield, then the failure condition applies.' Here every subfield HAS a non-empty programmatically determined name ('Card number'), so check #1 is TRUE for all four -> under F86's literal text the page PASSES F86. The 'failed' verdict relies on the unwritten claim that four identical names fail 'the spirit' of distinguishing subfields. The doc is honest about this ('F86 semantic variant', 'even though each string is non-empty'), but the procedure quote does NOT mechanically support a 'failed' outcome.

Scenario/implementation mismatch: both the HTML comment (line 40-41 area) and the .md doc (lines 24, 40-41) claim 'auto-advance between boxes' / 'when focus jumps to the next box' compounds the failure, but the page contains NO JavaScript at all. Auto-advance is not implemented. Tab order from the inspect tool is plain linear (stops 1-4), confirming no JS focus management. The claimed compounding mechanism does not actually exist on the page (not load-bearing for the verdict, but it is an inaccurate part of the claimed mechanism).

Borderline human-judgment case by design: whether identical-but-non-empty names on ordered segments of ONE value constitutes a 4.1.2 failure is genuinely debatable (all four DO belong to the same 'Card number', so a single repeated name is arguably semantically defensible, unlike a phone-number area/prefix/suffix where the parts are distinct). The doc acknowledges this. Reasonable reviewers could label this 'passed' or 'cantTell' rather than 'failed'.

PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): the prompt's Claimed scenario describes a Japanese postal-code portal with aria-label='郵便番号' and selector '.zip .cell > input[aria-label="郵便番号"]'. The ACTUAL file is a 'Holloway & Pike Lettings' rental price-range filter using an en-dash <label> mechanism. The prompt selector matches NOTHING in the file (no .zip, no 郵便番号, no aria-label on any input). I evaluated the actual corpus file, which is correct and consistent internally with its own .md doc.

The prompt's 'Chrome AX tree confirms two textboxes both named 郵便番号' is FALSE for this file; the AX tree shows textbox names 'Price range' (#price-min) and '–' (#price-max). This refutes the prompt scenario but confirms the real page's mechanism.

Minor scenario realism note (real page): an en-dash <label> wired to #price-max is an unusual authoring mistake, but it is exactly F86 Example 3's documented pattern and the developer-persona rationale (autocompleted stray 'for') is plausible; not a defect.

PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (orchestration-level, not a page defect): The task prompt describes a cardiology blood-pressure page (Northgate Cardiology, systolic/diastolic inputs + unit <select>, all named via title="Blood pressure", selector .bp input.num[title="Blood pressure"], ARIA14 citation). The actual case-05.html is a Posthaven Courier delivery-phone page (country/area/local-number inputs named by placeholder masks +##/###/#### ####, citing F111+F86). None of the prompt's claimed scenario, selector, mechanism (title-as-name), or ARIA14 citation exists in this file. The prompt's claimed ARIA14 citation could not be verified against this page because it belongs to a different page. Reviewed the actual file per METHOD step 1 (source-primary).

MINOR (F111 applicability nuance): F111's procedure scopes 'controls with a visible label'. The per-part captions are bare <span>s positioned as labels; they are de-facto visible labels for sighted users, so check #1 is true and check #3 (accessible name contains visible label text) is false -> fails. The reasoning is sound, but a strict reader could argue the unassociated span is not a formal 'visible label' in F111's enumerated examples; F86 (no name per part of a multi-part field) is the cleaner, unambiguous citation and is also present.

Scenario/doc calls this a 'PASS boundary contrast' page; there is no WCAG 1.4.3 contrast concern (computed color rgb(0,0,0) on rgb(255,255,255) = maximal). 'Contrast' here means a passing foil vs. the failing cases, not color contrast. Cosmetic wording only, consistent with the .md which clarifies it as the aspect contrast.
